locator: VII, lect. 1 nn. 886-889: whatever is moved is moved by some other
interpretation: Aquinas reconstructs Aristotle's proof (n. 886): a mobile supposed to move itself primarily and per se is divisible; if a part rests the whole rests; what rests on another's resting is moved by that other. Against Avicenna's objection he reads the premise as a true conditional (n. 889) and calls the proof propter quid: to move oneself is to be the first cause of one's own motion, and no divisible mobile has a motion that does not depend on its parts. Read as: whatever is being moved is moved by something other than itself, because nothing divisible moves itself primarily and per se. This is the whole-mobile principle of Physics VII; it is not relativized to respects, unlike STMT-WHATEVER-IS-MOVED-IS-MOVED-BY-ANOTHER (ST I q.2 a.3), and n. 890 notes it holds for motion as the act of a thing in potency, not for operations such as understanding. Basis: the English translation named in the passage manifest; a candidate for upgrade once a pinned Latin witness exists, and never a ground for overriding a reading of the Leonine/SCTA Latin.
